![A small sample of the stray/outdoor cats in Berkeley that I have met over the years!](../Berk_cats.png){style="text-align: center;" width="564"}

Berkeley is a truly wonderful city. Over the last 5 years, I have enjoyed many aspects of living here - the food, the weather, the geography. Oh, and not to mention ... the CATS. Berkeley, for some reason, seems to have an extremely high proportion of outdoor/stray cats. I love it.

Each neighborhood I have lived in has it's own unique clowder of cats. Some of them friendly, some of them standoff-ish, all of them delightful. Let's ball-park estimate the number of outdoor cats in Berkeley. Berkeley is roughly a square city, measuring 5x5 miles, and lets assume that there are 10 blocks in a city mile and lets also assume that each city block has at minimum 1 outdoor/stray cat. That gives us:

$$
25miles^2 * 10^2 \frac{blocks}{mile^2} * 10^0 \frac{cats}{block}=2,500 cats
$$

At minimum, there are 2,500 stray/outdoor cats in Berkeley. My personal experience tells me the true number must be a lot higher.

It is no surprise that the animal shelter in Berkeley is ["swamped" with kittens](https://www.berkeleyside.org/2022/07/13/berkeley-animal-shelter-overcrowded-with-cats). So, if you, like me, want to make sure all of these cats get into good homes, head down to the [Berkeley animal shelter!](https://berkeleyca.gov/community-recreation/animal-care-services/adopt-pet)

For fun, if we assume that each cat is a rectangle, measuring roughly 1 meter x 0.5 meter x 0.5 meter (think Maine Coon) giving 2.5m^2^ of surface area, and we estimate that each cm^2^ of cat surface has 1000 hairs inside of it:

$$
 2.5 m^2 * \frac{100^2 cm^2}{1 m^2} * 1000 \frac{hairs}{cm^2} * 2500 cats = 6.25e10hairs
$$ That is a lot of cat hair. Luckily, at any given time most of it stays on their body. If we very conservatively estimate that each cat sheds 10% of its hair in a given year (it probably sheds almost all of it?), then we are left with 6.25e9 cat hairs just floating around in the air on December 31st. Now imagine the winds align and push all this hair to Peoples Park. With random orientation, I estimate you lose most of the packing efficiency of cat hair, and I estimate we can now fit $$100 \frac{hairs}{cm^3}$$, resulting in $$
6.25e9hairs * \frac{1cm^3}{100 hairs} = 6.25e7cm^3
$$ Converting back to meters, we could pack all of those cat hairs into a box that is roughly 4x4x4 meters. It would be quite terrifying to see that inside of People's Park. Below is a hyper-realistic rendering of what that might look like.

![](/grok_cat_xmas.jpg){style="text-align: center;" width="198"}

To make sure this DOES NOT happen, next time you see a stray cat, pick it up and bring it home with you.
